subject: Chemistry
title: Belladonna: The Beautiful Killer
description: A micro-lesson that makes Belladonna: The Beautiful Killer usable.

hook.text: Renaissance women dropped deadly nightshade juice into their eyes to dilate their pupils and look beautiful.

buildup.text: Belladonna means 'beautiful woman' in Italian. The plant contains atropine, a potent alkaloid.

discovery.text: Atropine blocks acetylcholine receptors in the parasympathetic nervous system. Pupils dilate, heart races.

twist.text: Eat just a few berries and hallucinations begin. Ten berries can kill a child. It was a favorite of assassins.

climax.text: Doctors still use atropine today—to dilate pupils during eye exams and to restart stopped hearts.

punchline.text: The same chemical that killed can save. Dose makes the poison.

quiz.question: Why did Renaissance women use belladonna eye drops?
options: Atropine dilates pupils, which was considered beautiful

details.summary: Atropa belladonna contains atropine, an anticholinergic alkaloid that dilates pupils, accelerates heart rate, and at higher doses causes hallucinations, seizures, and death. Renaissance women used diluted drops to dilate their pupils for beauty, hence the name 'beautiful lady.'
details.whyItMatters: Atropine derived from belladonna is now a critical emergency medicine drug used to treat nerve agent poisoning, slow heart rhythms, and as a pre-surgical medication to reduce secretions.
takeaways: Belladonna's atropine blocks parasympathetic nervous system signals
Renaissance women used it cosmetically to dilate their pupils
Atropine is essential in treating nerve agent and pesticide poisoning

faq.question: How does atropine work as an antidote for nerve agent poisoning?
faq.answer: Nerve agents cause excessive acetylcholine buildup. Atropine blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, counteracting the effects of excess acetylcholine on glands, smooth muscle, and the heart. It does not reactivate the inhibited enzyme but blocks its downstream effects.

faq.question: How common is accidental belladonna poisoning today?
faq.answer: Accidental poisonings still occur, especially in children who eat the attractive berries. Belladonna grows wild across Europe and North America. All parts of the plant are toxic. Cases are treated with physostigmine, which counteracts atropine's anticholinergic effects.
